16 writers, 24 hrs—authors get on a Japanese train to finish a novel together

Each writer on the Twilight Express Mizukaze was given one chapter to write. The authors had discussed the basic story before boarding the train, but the writing had to happen during the journey.

Tarini Unnikrishnan
23 October, 2026 04:38 pm IST
Facebook
Twitter
WhatsApp
Linkedin
    Follow Us :
    Text Size:
    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 2:32
    Instaread

    Mumbai: Sixteen writers got on a train in Kyoto on Thursday with a plan to finish a novel together before they reached Matsue in western Japan the next morning. They had less than 24 hours to write around 200 pages collectively.

    Eight of the writers were Japanese and eight French-speaking. Each was given one chapter to write. They had discussed the basic story before boarding the train, but the writing had to happen during the journey, reported Japan Today.

    The project was organised by L’écriture en mouvement, or Writing in Motion, a French association that promotes literary exchanges.

    French novelist Muriel Barbery, who was among the writers, called it “a completely crazy project”.

    She explained that each writer was given a character to write about. All the characters know one person, and that person is the reason they are travelling together. The novel is set on the train itself.

    The writers boarded the Twilight Express Mizukaze, an Art Deco-style luxury sleeper train. There were also interpreters on board to help the Japanese and French-speaking writers communicate.

    Also read: Van Gogh’s Starry Night is a real night sky from 1889, finds new Korean study

    ‘Building bridges’

    Anne Forrest-Wilson, who founded Writing in Motion, was helping the writers bring their chapters together. The idea was to produce one novel rather than 16 separate stories.

    “I’m working to build bridges between the different pieces,” she told AFP.

    She said some of the Japanese and French writers had already started agreeing on ideas after discussing them and making drawings together.

    Other writers taking part include Japanese novelist Hitomi Kanehara, poet Machi Tawara, and French author Hervé Le Tellier, who won the Prix Goncourt in 2020 for The Anomaly.

    Le Tellier compared writing the novel together to “synchronised swimming”, where everyone has to coordinate with one another.

    Japanese science-fiction writer Toh EnJoe, who won the Akutagawa Prize in 2012, was writing in the train’s bar with a glass of wine when AFP spoke to him. He wasn’t sure the writers would be able to bring all their chapters together, since everyone was writing their part separately.

    The book is expected to be published in Japanese and French in 2027. EnJoe, meanwhile, had an unusual character to work with.

    “My protagonist is someone who missed the train,” he told AFP.

    A similar event was held in Canada in 2015. Twenty-four French-speaking writers travelled by train from Halifax to Toronto, writing a book about French explorer Samuel de Champlain. The resulting book, Sur les traces de Champlain, was published later that year and presented at the Montreal Book Fair. 

    (Edited by Aamaan Alam Khan)
